title: Review: Particles, isotopes and relative atomic mass; Emission spectra and energy levels; Orbitals and electron configuration; Ionisation energies
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AS04#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS04#t1 term and clue written for the game; AS04#t2 term and clue written for the game; AS03#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS01#N.15, AS03#N.12, AS04#N.3a, AS05#N.4a, AS01#N.5a, AS03#N.9, AS04#N.12a, AS05#N.2, AS01#N.7a, AS03#N.3a, AS04#N.9a, AS05#N.7a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Orbital
items.clue: A region around the nucleus where an electron is likely to be found; not a path.

items.label: Hund's rule
items.clue: Electrons enter regions of equal energy singly, with parallel spins, before pairing.

items.label: Shell
items.clue: A main electron level, numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4 outwards, holding at most 2n² electrons.

questions.stem: Bromine's relative atomic mass is 79.90, almost exactly halfway between 79 and 81. What does this show?

options.text: Most bromine atoms are bromine-80, with 45 neutrons each.
Every bromine atom has the same mass, 79.90, between those of its two isotopes.
Bromine is a mixture of bromine-79 and bromine-81 atoms in roughly equal numbers.
Bromine's electrons add 0.90 to the mass of each bromine-79 atom.

questions.explanation: 50.7% ⁷⁹Br and 49.3% ⁸¹Br weight the two masses almost equally: (78.918 × 50.69 + 80.916 × 49.31) ÷ 100 = 79.90.

questions.stem: Lithium compounds give a crimson-red flame. Sodium compounds give a yellow-orange flame. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Lithium's electrons fall across a larger energy gap, because red light has the longer wavelength.
The flame is hotter around sodium, so the same transitions give out higher-energy light.
Sodium's excited electrons fall across a larger energy gap, so each photon has more energy.
Sodium's electrons give out yellow photons as the flame raises them to higher levels.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that a 3d sub-shell can hold, and why?

options.text: 20 electrons, as its ten orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
18 electrons, as the n = 3 shell holds a maximum of 2n² electrons
10 electrons, as its five orbitals can each hold two electrons of opposite spin
2 electrons, as the 3d sub-shell is one orbital that holds a single pair

questions.explanation: Five orbitals × two electrons of opposite spin = 10.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of calcium?

options.text: Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻
Ca(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻
Ca⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + e⁻
Ca(s) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻

questions.explanation: One mole of electrons removed from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

questions.stem: An ion X³⁺ contains 23 electrons and 30 neutrons. Which nuclear symbol represents this ion? (Each symbol is written with its superscript first and its subscript second.)

options.text: ⁵⁰₂₀X³⁺
⁵³₂₃X³⁺
⁵⁶₂₆X³⁺
²⁶₅₆X³⁺

questions.explanation: Protons = 23 + 3 = 26 = Z. Mass number = 26 + 30 = 56. (X is iron.)

questions.stem: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
A ground-state phosphorus atom is [Ne] 3s² 3p³. Where are its three 3p electrons?

options.text: Together in one 3p orbital, which all three share.
On one circular orbit at a fixed distance from the nucleus.
Two paired in one 3p orbital, one in a second, the third left empty.
One in each of the three 3p orbitals, with parallel spins.

questions.explanation: Three equal-energy orbitals, three electrons: one each, spins parallel. Each electron is spread over its dumbbell-shaped region.

questions.stem: In the emission spectrum of hydrogen, the set of lines produced by electrons falling to n = 1 has its lowest-frequency line at a wavelength of 121.6 nm and converges to a limit at a wavelength of 91.18 nm. What is the first ionisation energy of hydrogen? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; E = hf; c = λf)

options.text: 983.8 kJ mol⁻¹
1312 kJ mol⁻¹
1.312 × 10⁶ kJ mol⁻¹
2.179 × 10⁻²¹ kJ mol⁻¹

questions.stem: Chlorine (atomic number 17) has isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. Pure samples of ³⁵Cl₂ gas and ³⁷Cl₂ gas are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ³⁷Cl₂ gas diffuses more slowly than ³⁵Cl₂.
The two gases diffuse at the same rate as each other.
The two gases undergo different chemical reactions.
The ³⁷Cl₂ molecules contain more electrons than ³⁵Cl₂.

questions.explanation: At the same temperature the heavier ³⁷Cl₂ molecules move more slowly on average. Diffusion rate is a physical property.

questions.stem: When sodium compounds are heated in a flame, the flame turns yellow. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this yellow light?

options.text: Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons.
Electrons absorb energy and emit photons as they rise to higher levels.
Electrons escape from the atoms entirely, releasing energy as photons.
The hot atoms glow with the yellow colour that sodium atoms possess.

questions.explanation: Each fall emits a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels; sodium's main gap gives yellow light.

questions.stem: An iron atom (Z = 26) has the condensed electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². How is an Fe²⁺ ion formed from this atom?

options.text: Two of the six 3d electrons are removed from the atom.
One 4s electron and one 3d electron are each removed.
Two electrons are added to the 3d sub-shell of the atom.
Both of the 4s electrons are removed from the atom.

questions.explanation: Transition metal atoms lose 4s electrons before 3d: [Ar] 3d⁶, 24 electrons.

questions.stem: How does the first ionisation energy generally change across Period 3 from sodium to argon, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among more and more electrons.
It decreases, as the atoms get larger because more electrons are added along the period.
It increases, as atoms closer to a full outer shell resist losing any of their outer electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons have similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Nuclear charge +11 to +18; the electron removed is in the third shell, with similar shielding. 496 → 1521 kJ mol⁻¹.
